opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. My honest take is that the architectural innovation is real, but it's more incremental than people might expect. If you put a modern open-weight model next to the original GPT-2 architecture, the resemblance is still striking. It's still a decoder-only transformer: you stack transformer blocks, you have attention and a feed-forward module, and you predict the next token. That core recipe has been remarkably durable.

What's changed is a long list of refinements that add up. Positional embeddings went from absolute to rotary embeddings (RoPE). LayerNorm largely became RMSNorm, and people experiment with where to put the normalization layers, pre-norm versus post-norm, plus things like QK-norm for training stability. The feed-forward modules moved from GELU to gated variants like SwiGLU. Multi-head attention evolved into grouped-query attention, and in some models multi-head latent attention, mostly to shrink the KV cache and make inference cheaper. Sliding-window attention shows up again, often interleaved with global attention layers.

The biggest structural shift is probably mixture-of-experts. Many of the leading open models are now MoE, so you get a very large total parameter count but only activate a fraction per token. That's a big deal for the efficiency-to-capability tradeoff, though conceptually it's still a transformer with the feed-forward layer swapped for a set of experts and a router.

The area I find most interesting heading into 2026 is the hybrids: models that replace some of the full attention layers with linear-attention or state-space-style layers, like gated DeltaNet variants, while keeping a few full attention layers. The motivation is long-context efficiency, because quadratic attention cost gets painful with very long contexts and agentic workloads. I wouldn't say these have dethroned the standard transformer yet, but they're credible, and we're seeing them in serious releases rather than only in research papers.

So if I zoom out, most of the progress in capability hasn't come from radical new architectures. It's come from better and more data, much better post-training, especially reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards for reasoning, and inference-time scaling, letting the model think longer. Architecture is increasingly about efficiency: cheaper inference, longer context, better hardware utilization. That's not unimportant. Efficiency is what makes these models deployable, but it's evolution rather than revolution.

My prediction is that we'll keep seeing that pattern for a while: tweaks to attention, more hybrid designs, smarter MoE routing. Then maybe at some point something like diffusion-based language models or a genuinely different paradigm will mature enough to compete. But I wouldn't bet on the transformer being replaced wholesale in the near term.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. It's a fun question because I think there are two honest answers, and they pull in opposite directions.

The first answer is: not that much has changed. If you take GPT-2 from 2019 and put it next to the leading open-weight models today, the skeleton is the same. It's still a decoder-only transformer, still next-token prediction, still attention plus a feed-forward block, repeated. If you squint, a lot of the "innovation" is swapping components in and out of that skeleton. LayerNorm became RMSNorm, absolute positional embeddings became RoPE, GELU became SwiGLU, and the normalization got moved around a bit. Individually, each of those is a modest change. So in that sense, I'd say the field has been remarkably conservative at the architectural level, and most of the capability gains came from scale, data, and post-training rather than from the architecture itself.

The second answer is that if you look at the details, 2025 was actually one of the more interesting years architecturally in a while, mostly because everyone got serious about efficiency. The clearest example is mixture of experts. A few years ago MoE was something Google and Mistral did and most people treated it as a curiosity. Now it's close to the default for frontier-scale open models. DeepSeek-V3 and R1 really changed the conversation there, with a large number of small experts plus a shared expert, and then you saw Llama 4, Qwen3, Kimi K2, gpt-oss all go that direction. The appeal is simple: you can have a very large total parameter count for knowledge capacity while keeping the active parameter count per token manageable for inference cost.

The other big theme is attention efficiency. Grouped-query attention was already standard, but DeepSeek's multi-head latent attention is a genuinely nice idea, compressing the KV cache into a lower-dimensional latent space rather than just sharing heads. And then you have the sliding-window attention revival in models like Gemma 3 and gpt-oss, where most layers use local attention and only a few use global attention. Again, that's about KV cache memory, not about raw modeling power. Beyond that you see things like QK-norm and attention sinks showing up more, which are small changes but they matter for training stability at scale.

The thing I find most interesting heading into 2026 is the stuff at the edges of the transformer. Qwen3-Next and Kimi Linear mixing in linear attention or gated DeltaNet style layers, so you get a hybrid where most layers are sub-quadratic and only a fraction are full attention. Those aren't fully replacing attention, but they're a sign that people are willing to deviate from the pure transformer when the economics push hard enough. Whether that becomes mainstream or stays a niche, I think we'll know within the next year or so.

And there are more exotic directions I'd put in the "promising but unproven" bucket. Text diffusion models, like Gemini Diffusion, which generate tokens in parallel rather than autoregressively. And then the various attempts to get recurrence or test-time compute into the architecture itself rather than just via longer chain-of-thought at inference.

So to sum up my assessment: at the conceptual level, we're still living in the transformer era and I don't see that changing in 2026. But at the engineering level, the gap between a 2023 architecture and a late-2025 architecture is real, and almost all of it is driven by inference cost rather than by trying to make the model fundamentally smarter. If I had to bet, the biggest architectural story of 2026 is going to be hybrids, some combination of MoE, mostly-local or linear attention, and a small number of expensive global layers, rather than something that replaces the transformer wholesale.

astra-6.text:
I think it helps to separate architectural innovation from improvements to the overall system. A model can become substantially more capable without a fundamentally new architecture. Better training data, changes to the training recipe, post-training, and spending more compute at inference time can all make a big difference.

At the architectural level, my assessment is that it’s more evolutionary than revolutionary. There’s still a lot of room to improve how models use memory, how efficiently they handle context, and how much computation they activate for a given input. Those changes matter, even if they don’t replace the basic transformer framework.

The caveat is that we don’t have full visibility into all the leading models. If a model performs better, we can’t infer from that alone that it has a novel architecture. So heading into 2026, I’d be cautious about equating capability gains with architectural breakthroughs. The interesting question is how much each change contributes—and whether we can actually isolate that contribution.

r004.rationale: It notes that the transformer framework remains basic, but does not identify companies’ reuse of proven architectures as a preference over experimentation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s hard to assess from the outside, because we don’t have the architectural details for many of the leading models. We can observe that capabilities are improving, but that doesn’t tell us how much comes from architecture versus training data, compute, post-training, or inference-time techniques.

My sense is that a lot of the progress is still happening within the Transformer framework. There can be substantial engineering innovation in attention, mixture-of-experts routing, or how you use memory without replacing the whole architecture. Those changes matter, especially if they let you train or serve a model more efficiently.

So heading into 2026, I would distinguish between architectural novelty and capability gains. A better model isn’t necessarily evidence of a fundamentally new architecture. I’d want to see controlled comparisons—similar data, similar compute budgets—before attributing the improvement to a particular architectural change. For the closed models, we often just don’t have that evidence.
